A heroine is a woman who is deeply admired — either for her bravery and good deeds in real life, or as the main female character in a story.

1. A woman of courage, nobility, or great deeds (in real life)

This is a woman who does something remarkable — something that takes courage, sacrifice, or exceptional moral strength. People look up to her. She is celebrated because her actions go beyond what ordinary people do, especially in the face of danger, hardship, or injustice.

She doesn't have to wear a cape or have superpowers. A heroine can be:

  • A soldier who risks her life to protect others
  • A woman who stands up against injustice when everyone else stays silent
  • A doctor who works in a war zone to save the wounded
  • A mother who makes extraordinary sacrifices for her children

The word carries a sense of admiration and moral goodness. A heroine is not just strong — she uses her strength for something worthy and noble.

"Malala Yousafzai is regarded as a heroine by millions around the world."

2. The main female character in a story

In a novel, film, play, or any work of fiction, the heroine is the central woman — the female lead — around whom the story revolves. She is the character the audience follows most closely, cares about most deeply, and whose journey drives the plot.

This is the literary meaning of the word.

"Elizabeth Bennet is the heroine of Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice."
"The heroine of the film must choose between her duty and her love."

A story's heroine is typically someone the audience is meant to root for. She faces challenges, struggles, grows, and often triumphs in the end — or her failure carries the emotional weight of the story. Think of her as the story's beating heart.

"Heroine" can also refer to a woman who is someone's personal inspiration — a role model, someone they deeply admire and look up to, even if the world at large doesn't know her name.

"My grandmother is my heroine. She raised five children alone and never complained."

Here, the word expresses deep personal admiration. Your heroine is the woman who inspires you.

"Hero" is the masculine form and "heroine" is the feminine form of the same idea. Traditionally:

  • A man of courage = hero
  • A woman of courage = heroine

However, in modern English, "hero" is increasingly used as a gender-neutral word — so it is perfectly acceptable and common today to call a woman a "hero" as well. Saying "she is a hero" sounds completely natural. "Heroine" still exists and is used, but it is the more traditionally gendered choice.

The plural of heroine is heroines.

This is one of the most important things to know about this word, because the confusion can be embarrassing:

  • Heroine (with an e at the end) = the word you just learned — a brave woman or female protagonist.
  • Heroin (without the e) = a highly addictive and dangerous illegal drug.

They look almost identical, but they mean completely different things. Always double-check the spelling:

✅ "The heroine of the story saved the village." (brave woman)
❌ "The heroin of the story saved the village." (nonsense — and alarming)

The safest habit: if you mean a brave woman or a fictional female lead, make sure you write the e at the end.

The word "heroine" is about a woman who is worthy of admiration — whether she earned that through real bravery in the world, or through being the soul of a story told on a page or screen.
